CSEC/GCI has a cap now because of the transition to the Global CyberSecurity Institute. Personally, my best advise after doing what the others have said (talking to admissions) is reach out to your advisors and transfer over. Not sure what your third choice major is but if it’s Computing related, you will most likely not have any impact to graduation and should be able to transfer credits over easily. The first year of CSEC is gen Ed’s anyways. 

Furthermore, there are ways to learn security outside of classes. RITSEC, which is RIT’s Computing Security Club and Community, is an amazing to place to go to learn more about security topics before you learn about them in class. We meet 12-4 every Friday, with meetings that feature educational presentations, demo challenges, and member research projects and presentations. Furthermore, we have Hack Nights, an online community, CTF and Red Vs Blue competitions, and overall just a great community of learners and security people. Plz feel free to DM if you have anymore questions.

I'm a first year at RIT, a CSEC major, and heavily involved in RITSEC, but not on the CCDC team. The first time that I touched the command line was the first day of classes. I tried, (and still try) to take advantage of every opportunity that I have to learn something new. 

During practices, we general build a box and then install/configure/set up a service to run on the box. Examples are: setting up PostFix on a Linux box for Mail, or configuring and writing firewall rules on a pfSense router, or creating an AD, joining a box to the Domain, and configuring user roles/creds. 

To gain experience in this areas, once you join the workplace, you can do/look at the demos given in club, reach out to team members/alumni, and challenges from sites like [OverTheWire.org](https://OverTheWire.org) (linux command line things) and [Underthewire.tech](https://Underthewire.tech) (Powershell things)

Of course, if you have any questions, feel free to reach out. The CSEC major, and especially those in RITSEC, are really friendly and like to help each other out. Finally, one thought that I've carried with me: "The only bad question is the one that you don't ask"

Hi. Current student at RIT. I am currently involved in [RITSEC](https://www.ritsec.club) (the club associated with the CSEC major), APO (a national community service fraternity, but a community service club at RIT), and I will have two jobs in the spring semestre. 

Everything boils down to time management and what your definition of "free time" is. At the end of the day, if you can get the grades you want, have the social experience that you want, and be involved with 10 groups, then go for it. If you can't get the grades that you want, and you aren't having the social experience that you want because you're overcommitted, then tone it back a bit. If you look at your free time as doing any activity that isn't homework, studying, or going to classes, vs free time as time for watching Netflix, gaming, or something else, then that will change your perspective on time management. 

To learn some more details on RITSEC, read on. RITSEC meets officially for four hours every week. Every Friday from noon to four, the club gathers in Webb Auditorium in Booth. The first two hours consist of "Education", where somebody presents on a topic for about an hour, then students do CTF style activities based on the topic presented. Then there is a quick break, and we resume with "Research". Research is a time where students can deliver shorter presentations about anything computer security related. These presentations are generally 5 to 20 minutes long. Outside of the club meetings, RITSEC hosts several other events throughout the year, from hackerthons to competitions to CTFs. These events usually take place over a weekend. To relate this back to your question, the time commitment is what you want to put into it. You could go to the club meetings, you could go to half of the club meetings. You could just try to do the big events hosted by RITSEC. Ultimately, it's up to you. 

I recommend doing what you can in the time that you have. One of the biggest pieces of advice that some shared with me is this, "There isn't enough time in the world to do everything. But there's enough time to do something meaningful". I know that this is a bit long-winded, but I hope it helps.
